headline: Five signals were public before or during the drain; the issuer freezes were what worked
dek: Five signals were public before or during the drain. Preventing the first sweep required a transaction included in the 204-second window after the delegation; later action could have blocked part of the outflows that followed, given monitoring and signing access.

key_numbers.label: first rehearsal to the Binance 14 delegation
from Whale Alert's 20:06 XRP post to the Ethereum delegation
moved on explorer-visible lines after the 20:32 post

narrative: Signal one: the rehearsal, 6 hours 29 minutes before the delegation; the first contract had been on-chain since 02:28. From 13:51 UTC a fresh address funded only by Tornado Cash delegated two dust wallets to an unverified contract with a sweep(address, address[]) selector, seeded them with a few dollars of USDT and USDC, and swept them. At 16:20 it repeated the run with the second contract: hardcoded operator, leave-one-ether logic, a withdraw. None of it touched a Binance address.

The pattern (mixer-funded sponsor, type-4 delegation to unverified code, sweep selector, dust wallets) matches the drainer behavior wallet-security vendors describe in their 7702 write-ups. A rule for 'type-4 transaction sponsored by a Tornado-funded address, delegating to unverified code' fires at 13:51:35; the full pattern is complete by 14:24. It would not have named Binance as the target. It would have put 0x7C86 on a watchlist that hit again at 20:20:59.

Signal two: the cross-chain start. Whale Alert posted 185,017,485 XRP ($236M) leaving Binance for an 'unknown new wallet' at 20:06 and 965,455 SOL ($95M) to another new wallet at 20:11. The posts drew 59K and 45K engagements and passed as routine; in the sampled posts nobody linked them to anything until @hackenclub at 20:51. @ai_9684xtpa's Chinese-language summary at 00:00 put the first suspicious hot-wallet outflow at 04:10 Beijing, 20:10 UTC.

An exchange can run 'hot wallet to never-seen address, above $50M, on two chains, within ten minutes' against its own signing logs. On Whale Alert's post times that rule fires at 20:11, ten minutes before the Ethereum delegation; on an exchange's own logs, earlier. It also fires on routine cold-wallet rotations, so it is a review trigger, not a kill switch. Whether the XRP and SOL moves were the attacker's or Binance's own is unresolved; the transfers are on-chain, and only their attribution to Binance rests on Whale Alert's label.

Signal three: 3 minutes 24 seconds, seventeen blocks, between delegation (20:20:59) and sweep (20:24:23). A monitor that decodes type-4 transactions in new blocks and matches authorization signers against an exchange's own wallets fires at inclusion. No public account mentioned the delegation until @odysseas_eth at 20:54, thirty minutes after the sweep.

The window allowed a competing type-4 transaction from Binance 14 clearing the delegation, the kind Binance sent at 00:10, or moving balances out. Neither is guaranteed to land inside 17 blocks. A cleared delegation holds until another valid authorization is included on-chain; clearing the code does not invalidate authorizations already signed. An attacker can also put delegation and sweep in one transaction.

Signal four: the open delegation, where the later outflows can be counted. The 20:24 sweep took what Binance 14 held. Everything after moved through a delegation live until 00:10:35 and readable on-chain from inclusion (Etherscan showed a 'Delegate to' label). The 780M USDC at 20:41 and 43M at 20:59 moved because Hot Wallet 34 accepted calls from Binance 14; the 21:04 and 21:44 sweeps took value that arrived after the first sweep, including 200.4M USDT; the 22:39 sweep took long-tail tokens marked at about $7.5M on the ten largest lines the explorer lists.

The ledger: 780M + 43M + 3.9M + 200.4M + about 7.5M, about $1.03B on explorer-visible lines after @spreekaway's 20:32 post; about $255M of that after 20:41; about $208M plus unpriced lines after 21:15, fifty-one minutes after the sweep. A delegation cleared before 20:41 blocks all of it; cleared between 20:41 and 20:59, about $255M. Much of the USDT and USDC was later frozen, so not all of what moved is lost. Blockscout records 533 incoming token transfers to Binance 14 in the window.

Signal five: the mood of the day. Between 17:47 and 18:56 UTC, 84 to 153 minutes before the delegation, posts on X carried a wave of signing-attack news: 'Polymarket hacked, everyone withdraw now' (@TheNotoriousSKi, 144K), 'Polymarket frontend is injecting a malicious script to sell all your positions' (@aaalex, 188K), CZ on a Ledger supply-chain compromise in Singapore (435K) and, at 18:56, CZ describing 'an injection attack on the front end' (640K).

At 04:49 on Oct 28, CZ had listed four data leaks in one day. None of it named Binance's hot wallets, and front-end injection against retail users is a different class of attack from fifty authorization signatures on an exchange hot wallet.

The response that worked came from the issuers. @TreeNewsFeed reported Tether's $971M freeze at 21:05. Whale Alert then posted the freezes: 312.7M USDT on Tron at 21:10, 971M USDT on Ethereum at 21:11 and Circle's 823M USDC at 21:13, about $2.1B, all before Binance posted anything. Two more by 21:31 (66M and 175M USDT) took the feed's total to about $2.35B; Binance later put the verified frozen figure at $2.54B (23:22) and around $3B (00:52).

@odysseas_eth counted about 72 percent of the stablecoins that reached the sweep recipient frozen by 21:43 and, by the same count, 700M USDT already moved on. Yi He thanked Ripple for freezing 'approximately 200 million' and World Liberty for 27M USD1, and @zachxbt reported the Arbitrum Security Council recovering about $30M at midnight.

No freeze touches ETH or BTC. Whale Alert posted 195,460 ETH moving at 20:40 and about 16,690 BTC in four transfers between 20:30 and 20:33, and at 02:00 UTC the main receiver was converting long-tail tokens into ETH about once every twelve seconds; it was still swapping at 03:17 UTC. Freezes worked where the asset had an issuer and nowhere else.

callouts.title: Watch your own signatures
callouts.body: Decode every type-4 transaction in new blocks and match authorization signers against your own wallets: that alert fires at the delegation, not the sweep. Pair it with a rule that a wallet carrying delegated code receives no new inbound routing until the code is cleared.

callouts.title: The rehearsal is the tell
callouts.body: Mixer-funded fresh address, type-4 delegation to unverified code with a sweep selector, dust wallets seeded, swept and withdrawn: that pattern ran on mainnet from 13:51 UTC, and nobody published it until after the drain.

receipts.quote: 185,017,485 $XRP (235,816,974 USD) transferred from #Binance to unknown new wallet
...it appears to be an injection attack on the front end. injecting incorrect tx, but showing a valid tx for the user to sign.
THE REHEARSAL 02:28 UTC: the attacker deploys a sweeper contract... 13:51 to 16:47: they practise on their own fresh wallets. EIP 7702 delegation, then sweep.
You only get a stack of pre-signed auths like that if the key or the signing system is compromised. They tested the setup on other addresses throughout Oct 29.
All of crypto is getting pentested right now. If you are under-investing in AI security / pentesting, now is the time to fix that.

watch: Whether Binance's post-mortem covers inbound routing to Binance 14 during the 3h49m window; the 200.4M USDT swept at 21:44 is the test.
Confirmation that the 20:05 XRP and 20:10 SOL outflows were the attacker's would date the compromise before the Ethereum delegation.
A published, backtested rehearsal-pattern alert that would have fired at 13:51; every transaction it needs is public.
